Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Aligned Action Spaces
for Cross-Game Generalization

Jing Yi Affiliation: LIGHTSPEED    Cehao Yang Affiliation: HKUST(GZ)    Hualei Zhang Affiliation: HKUST    Haitao Li Affiliation: LIGHTSPEED
Abstract

Zero-shot cross-game generalization aims to consolidate accessible source-game experts into a single vision-language model (VLM) that controls unseen games from raw pixels without target-game parameter updates. While multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) mitigates offline exposure bias and single-game reinforcement learning (RL) overfitting, scaling it to autoregressive VLMs faces two bottlenecks. First, token-to-action misalignment from subword length bias distorts discrete action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Second, multi-teacher policy conflict arises as source teachers under incompatible dynamics issue contradictory closed-loop corrections, causing negative transfer. We propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), a post-training framework that resolves multi-teacher policy conflict within an aligned semantic action space. CAMOPD first uses complete-action alignment to normalize command completion likelihoods over each game’s legal action set, forming a calibrated categorical policy that provides reliable uncertainty margins for selective on-policy retention and visual specialist probes that can be evaluated across source games. To resolve policy conflict without target-game data, conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation cross-evaluates these specialists across source games to capture both visual identifiability and inter-teacher compatibility, upweighting compatible teachers while suppressing conflicting corrections. On GameWorld’s temporal and directional transfer suites with Qwen3.5-4B, CAMOPD achieves 26/30 (86.7%) and 24/30 (80.0%) Task-1 zero-shot success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, outperforming prompting, weight-merging, and multi-task baselines.

1 Introduction

Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly enable generalist agents to control interactive environments from raw pixels [27, 4, 17, 26, 38, 22], with GameWorld [23] standardizing state-verifiable browser-game evaluation. Beyond in-distribution training environments, open-ended deployment on user-generated content (UGC) platforms, indie web portals, and HTML5 mini-games requires cross-game generalization: transferring reusable visual-motor skills to unseen games without target-game parameter updates. Because accessing private simulator state or running per-game RL for every new title is infeasible at deployment, we consolidate source-game teachers into a single pixel-only student operating solely on screenshots and public instructions.

Adapting VLMs for zero-shot cross-game generalization faces challenges in both action grounding and closed-loop training. At the decision interface, autoregressive VLMs exhibit token-to-action misalignment: factorizing commands into variable-length subword sequences over an open vocabulary biases raw likelihoods toward shorter strings rather than optimal actions, distorting action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Furthermore, conventional post-training struggles under closed-loop transfer: offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT) compounds errors once the agent drifts into unfamiliar states [29], whereas traditional on-policy RL [32, 35] either requires costly trial-and-error in the target game or overfits to a single source game. Consolidating diverse source experts via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) [21] thus offers a natural paradigm to learn closed-loop recovery without target-game access.

However, scaling MOPD across heterogeneous source games exposes a critical bottleneck: multi-teacher policy conflict. Source games often obey incompatible control rules in visually similar situations—for example, steering toward foreground geometry to land on platforms (e.g., NS-Shaft) versus steering away from foreground blocks to dodge obstacles (e.g., Cubefield). Combining such contradictory teacher corrections indiscriminately—via uniform MOPD [21], gradient projection [43], or weight-space merging [14, 39, 42, 7, 15, 16, 10]—pulls the shared student in opposite directions and causes severe negative transfer. Identifying which teachers conflict without target-game data is also non-trivial: unlike language-domain MOPD where every large language model (LLM) teacher can score any text prompt [33], privileged game teachers read game-specific internal simulator variables (e.g., ball coordinates or tile grids) rather than raw pixels, so a teacher for one game cannot be executed on another game to measure inter-teacher agreement.

To address these challenges, we propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), which resolves multi-teacher conflict within an aligned semantic action space (Fig. 1). Rather than generating raw subwords, Complete-Action Alignment scores full legal commands per token to establish a calibrated student policy and visual specialist proxies for the privileged rule teachers. Selective On-Policy Retention then rolls out the student across source games, querying teachers only on uncertain or erroneous boundary states [45]. Finally, because visual specialists operate on pixels rather than private simulator variables, Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher Consolidation cross-evaluates them across peer source games to estimate teacher reliability and compatibility without target-game data. At deployment, all teachers and probes are discarded, leaving a single pixel-only Qwen3.5-4B policy evaluated zero-shot on GameWorld. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Complete-action alignment. We eliminate subword length bias via length-normalized candidate scoring over each game’s legal action set, yielding calibrated decision margins for selective on-policy retention and enabling pixel-only specialist probes across distinct action sets.

  • •

    Conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation. We formulate a target-free disagreement matrix by cross-evaluating source specialists, coupling in-game visual identifiability with cross-game control compatibility to reweight on-policy recovery gradients before consolidation.

  • •

    Zero-shot transfer and boundary analysis. CAMOPD reaches 86.7% and 80.0% Task-1 success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, surpassing standalone specialists, parameter mergers, and gradient surgery, while causal and cross-genre analyses characterize grounding and transfer boundaries.

2 Related Work

2.1 Generalist Game Agents and VLA Training

Prior multimodal game and vision-language-action (VLA) control spans three agent families and distinct benchmarks. (i) Large-scale trajectory pretraining: Gato [27], RT-2 [4], and OpenVLA [17] emit discretized control tokens, while SIMA [26], Game-TARS [38], and NitroGen [22] scale behavior cloning (BC) or continual pretraining from gameplay demonstrations (native keyboard–mouse trajectories or flow-matched gamepad chunks). (ii) Training-free prompting, such as Cradle [34], couples VLM reasoning with perception and pause-and-plan modules. (iii) Online RL post-training—RL4VLM [44], VAGEN [37], and Game-RL [35]—fine-tunes VLMs with environment rewards [32]. For evaluation, Orak [25] targets commercial games via Model Context Protocol (MCP) textual states and agentic tools, whereas GameWorld [23] benchmarks pixel-only control in paused browser sandboxes with state-verifiable progress. We adopt GameWorld’s pixel-only setting to study zero-shot consolidation of source teachers without massive video pretraining or target-game RL.

2.2 Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation

Offline distillation compresses RL policies [30, 24] or visual encoders (MoVE-KD [5]) on fixed data, whereas interactive imitation mitigates rollout drift via online queries (DAgger [29]), uncertainty gating (SafeDAgger [45]), or privileged-to-visual supervision [6]. In autoregressive models, on-policy distillation (OPD) similarly supervises student rollouts across language generation (MiniLLM [11], GKD [1]), VLM reasoning (VOLD [3]), and VLA control (VLA-OPD [46]). Multi-teacher variants aggregate domain experts (MOPD [21], MAD-OPD [36]) or mitigate conflict via token reliability (TrustMOPD [33]), subspace constraints (PMOPD [19]), and update projection (UP-MOPD [47]). Yet these methods assume homogeneous teachers over a shared vocabulary, whereas CAMOPD resolves conflict across heterogeneous game teachers via source-only visual probing.

2.3 Action Grounding, Merging, and Routing

Executable grounding constrains outputs via grammar decoding [31], candidate scoring [41], affordances [2], or uncertainty calibration [28]; we length-normalize candidate likelihoods to remove multi-token bias. To combine Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [12] adapters without target updates, static mergers—RegMean [16], Task Arithmetic [14], TIES [39], DARE [42], DELLA [7], Model Stock [15], and AdaMerging [40]—fuse weights, and TIME [9] merges sequential multimodal tasks. Alternatively, PCGrad [43] and CAGrad [18] project conflicting gradients, LoraHub [13] and Twin-Merging [20] compose LoRA modules at test time, MergeVLA [10] pairs task-masked merging with a test-time router, and HiMoE-VLA [8] co-trains hierarchical action-space Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs). However, these methods treat conflicting experts equally or rely on test-time routing, whereas CAMOPD asymmetrically consolidates teachers in action space into one student.

3 Method

CAMOPD consolidates heterogeneous source teachers into a single pixel-only VLM through three progressive components (Fig. 1; Algorithm 1 in Appendix A). Following the problem setup (Sec. 3.1), we detail Complete-Action Alignment (Sec. 3.2), Selective On-Policy Retention (Sec. 3.3), and Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher Consolidation (Sec. 3.4).

3.1 Problem Formulation

Source and target POMDPs.

Let 𝒢src={g1,…,gM}\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}=\{g_{1},\dots,g_{M}\} denote the set of MM source training games and let g⋆∉𝒢srcg^{\star}\notin\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}} denote an unseen held-out target game. Each game g∈𝒢src∪{g⋆}g\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}\cup\{g^{\star}\} is formulated as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) with simulator state st∈𝒮gs_{t}\in\mathcal{S}_{g}, raw RGB screenshot observation ot∈𝒪go_{t}\in\mathcal{O}_{g}, and finite legal semantic action set 𝒜g\mathcal{A}_{g}. The deployed student does not access private simulator state sts_{t}; at decision step tt, it receives the multimodal context xtx_{t} consisting of the last h∈{1,2}h\in\{1,2\} screenshots ot−h+1:t=(ot−h+1,…,ot)o_{t-h+1:t}=(o_{t-h+1},\dots,o_{t}) and the game’s public task instruction prompt qgq_{g} specifying 𝒜g\mathcal{A}_{g}:

xt=(ot−h+1:t,qg).x_{t}=(o_{t-h+1:t},q_{g}). (1)

Frame stacks (h=2h=2) provide velocity cues for steering, while single frames (h=1h=1) suffice for timing.

Privileged source teachers and held-out targets.

During source collection (g∈𝒢srcg\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}), each source game is paired with a programmatic rule teacher τg:𝒮g→𝒜g×(0,1]\tau_{g}:\mathcal{S}_{g}\to\mathcal{A}_{g}\times(0,1] that reads privileged state st∈𝒮gs_{t}\in\mathcal{S}_{g} and outputs reference action at⋆∈𝒜ga_{t}^{\star}\in\mathcal{A}_{g} and criticality confidence ct∈(0,1]c_{t}\in(0,1] (Appendix C). Rolling out τg\tau_{g} yields the initial SFT dataset 𝒟0=⋃g∈𝒢src𝒟g\mathcal{D}_{0}=\bigcup_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}}\mathcal{D}_{g} with 𝒟g={(xt,𝒜g,at⋆,ct)}t=1Ng\mathcal{D}_{g}=\{(x_{t},\mathcal{A}_{g},a_{t}^{\star},c_{t})\}_{t=1}^{N_{g}}, where training splits are used for policy updates and held-out action-balanced validation splits 𝒟gval\mathcal{D}_{g}^{\mathrm{val}} are reserved for cross-source conflict probing. Target transitions, screenshots, and rewards are excluded from policy updates, and teacher allocation weights are computed from source validation data alone.

3.2 Complete-Action Alignment

Length-normalized action scoring.

Because each game exposes a distinct legal action set 𝒜g\mathcal{A}_{g}, we align decisions in semantic action space rather than open-vocabulary token space. Standard autoregressive behavior cloning factorizes each command string into a variable-length subword sequence y⁡(a)=(y1,…,yLa)y(a)=(y_{1},\dots,y_{L_{a}}) of length LaL_{a} and optimizes token-level cross-entropy over an open language vocabulary, which tends to bias raw generation likelihoods toward shorter or lexically favored strings rather than optimal control actions. To align scoring with atomic executable decisions, we attach a shared LoRA adapter [12] with parameters θ\theta to the VLM attention and multilayer perceptron (MLP) projections and evaluate each legal command a∈𝒜ga\in\mathcal{A}_{g} as a complete semantic unit. Given multimodal context xx, we render the prompt under a deterministic non-thinking template (Appendix C) and construct |𝒜g||\mathcal{A}_{g}| candidate sequences by appending each structured JSON command completion y⁡(a)y(a). Masking prompt tokens, we compute the length-normalized completion score over all LaL_{a} tokens:

sθ(a∣x)=1La∑ℓ=1Lalogpθ(yℓ(a)|x,y<ℓ(a)),s_{\theta}(a\mid x)=\frac{1}{L_{a}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_{a}}\log p_{\theta}\!\left(y_{\ell}(a)\;\middle|\;x,y_{<\ell}(a)\right), (2)

where pθ​(yℓ​(a)∣x,y<ℓ​(a))p_{\theta}(y_{\ell}(a)\mid x,y_{<\ell}(a)) is the autoregressive completion probability. Masking prompt tokens avoids context dilution, while dividing by LaL_{a} scores short (e.g., wait) and multi-token (e.g., move_right) commands per token.

Categorical policy and model initialization.

Applying a softmax with temperature T>0T>0 over 𝒜g\mathcal{A}_{g} maps the command scores into a differentiable categorical policy πθ(T)\pi_{\theta}^{(T)} (πθ\pi_{\theta} at T=1T=1):

πθ(T)​(a∣x,𝒜g)=exp⁡(sθ​(a∣x)/T)∑a′∈𝒜gexp⁡(sθ​(a′∣x)/T).\pi_{\theta}^{(T)}(a\mid x,\mathcal{A}_{g})=\frac{\exp\!\left(s_{\theta}(a\mid x)/T\right)}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}_{g}}\exp\!\left(s_{\theta}(a^{\prime}\mid x)/T\right)}. (3)

Offline action-aligned SFT initializes the shared student adapter θSFT\theta_{\mathrm{SFT}} on 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} via complete-action negative log-likelihood (NLL):

ℒSFT​(θ)=𝔼(x,𝒜g,a⋆)∼𝒟0​[−log⁡πθ​(a⋆∣x,𝒜g)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,\mathcal{A}_{g},a^{\star})\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}}\left[-\log\pi_{\theta}(a^{\star}\mid x,\mathcal{A}_{g})\right]. (4)

In parallel, minimizing Eq. 4 on each single-game dataset 𝒟g\mathcal{D}_{g} yields a frozen visual specialist probe πTg​(a∣x,𝒜g)\pi_{T_{g}}(a\mid x,\mathcal{A}_{g}) that acts as a pixel-based proxy for τg\tau_{g} and can be evaluated on any peer game g′g^{\prime} over 𝒜g′\mathcal{A}_{g^{\prime}}.

Action-simplex gradients and margin calibration.

Differentiating Eq. 4 with respect to each candidate score sθ​(a∣x)s_{\theta}(a\mid x) (a∈𝒜ga\in\mathcal{A}_{g}, T=1T=1) yields

∂(−log⁡πθ​(a⋆∣x,𝒜g))∂sθ​(a∣x)=πθ(a∣x,𝒜g)−𝕀[a=a⋆].\frac{\partial\!\left(-\log\pi_{\theta}(a^{\star}\mid x,\mathcal{A}_{g})\right)}{\partial s_{\theta}(a\mid x)}=\pi_{\theta}(a\mid x,\mathcal{A}_{g})-\mathbb{I}[a=a^{\star}]. (5)

Standard token-level cross-entropy normalizes over the entire open vocabulary at every subword step, diluting gradients across non-executable tokens and biasing likelihoods by length LaL_{a}. In contrast, Eq. 5 restricts competition to the legal action set 𝒜g\mathcal{A}_{g}: raising sθ​(a⋆∣x)s_{\theta}(a^{\star}\mid x) directly pushes down each competing command a≠a⋆a\neq a^{\star} in proportion to its probability πθ​(a∣x,𝒜g)\pi_{\theta}(a\mid x,\mathcal{A}_{g}). Dividing by LaL_{a} also calibrates top-two score margins on a per-token scale, providing a length-unbiased confidence signal to identify low-margin boundary states for selective on-policy retention (Sec. 3.3). Moreover, unlike fixed-dimension action heads, scoring command strings via the shared VLM head constructs πθ(⋅∣x,𝒜g⋆)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\mathcal{A}_{g^{\star}}) for any unseen target game g⋆g^{\star} without target-head retraining.

3.3 Selective On-Policy Retention

Offline demonstrations 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} cover only teacher-visited trajectories, leaving the student susceptible to compounding drift on unfamiliar test-time states [29]. Within MOPD, we roll out the shared student πθ\pi_{\theta} across source games g∈𝒢srcg\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}. At each visited state xtx_{t}, the student executes a^t=arg⁡maxa∈𝒜g​πθ​(a∣xt,𝒜g)\hat{a}_{t}=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{g}}\pi_{\theta}(a\mid x_{t},\mathcal{A}_{g}) with calibrated margin mθ​(xt)=sθ​(a^t∣xt)−maxa∈𝒜g∖{a^t}⁡sθ​(a∣xt)≥0m_{\theta}(x_{t})=s_{\theta}(\hat{a}_{t}\mid x_{t})-\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{g}\setminus\{\hat{a}_{t}\}}s_{\theta}(a\mid x_{t})\geq 0, while the game-matched rule teacher τg​(st)\tau_{g}(s_{t}) returns reference action at⋆a_{t}^{\star} and confidence ctc_{t}. Rather than retaining all rollout frames as in standard DAgger [29], a transition enters the on-policy correction buffer 𝒬g\mathcal{Q}_{g} [45] when the teacher is confident (ct≥cmin>0c_{t}\geq c_{\min}>0) and the student either errs (a^t≠at⋆\hat{a}_{t}\neq a_{t}^{\star}) or exhibits a low margin (mθ​(xt)<δm_{\theta}(x_{t})<\delta):

ℐretain(xt,st)=𝕀[ct≥cmin]⋅𝕀[a^t≠at⋆∨mθ(xt)<δ].\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{retain}}(x_{t},s_{t})=\mathbb{I}[c_{t}\geq c_{\min}]\cdot\mathbb{I}\!\left[\hat{a}_{t}\neq a_{t}^{\star}\;\lor\;m_{\theta}(x_{t})<\delta\right]. (6)

Here ct≥cminc_{t}\geq c_{\min} filters out incomplete or degenerate simulator states, while a^t≠at⋆∨mθ​(xt)<δ\hat{a}_{t}\neq a_{t}^{\star}\lor m_{\theta}(x_{t})<\delta omits routine agreement frames (80%–90% of rollout steps) to retain student-induced errors and near-boundary states. Because the retained set 𝒬=⋃g∈𝒢src𝒬g\mathcal{Q}=\bigcup_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}}\mathcal{Q}_{g} accounts for at most 10%10\% of the combined data (Table 1), training on 𝒬\mathcal{Q} alone risks forgetting nominal control, so we consolidate on 𝒟0∪𝒬\mathcal{D}_{0}\cup\mathcal{Q}.

3.4 Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher Consolidation

Multi-teacher gradient conflict in uniform MOPD.

When training on 𝒟0∪𝒬\mathcal{D}_{0}\cup\mathcal{Q}, we amplify retained corrections i∈𝒬i\in\mathcal{Q} by an on-policy weight wq≥1w_{q}\geq 1 so this small boundary set is not overwhelmed by 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0}. However, uniform MOPD [21] treats all source teachers equally by applying the same wqw_{q} across every g∈𝒢srcg\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}: it updates θ\theta along v¯0​(θ)+wq​∑g∈𝒢srcv¯g​(θ)\bar{v}_{0}(\theta)+w_{q}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}}\bar{v}_{g}(\theta), combining the aggregated action-loss gradient v¯0​(θ)\bar{v}_{0}(\theta) on offline demonstrations 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} with each teacher’s on-policy recovery gradient v¯g​(θ)\bar{v}_{g}(\theta) on 𝒬g\mathcal{Q}_{g}. By the chain rule on Eq. 5, when an incompatible teacher g−g^{-} and a compatible teacher g+g^{+} prescribe opposing actions in visually similar states (e.g., steering toward platforms in NS-Shaft vs. away from blocks in Cubefield), they drive action scores in opposite directions and induce conflicting gradients (⟨v¯g−​(θ),v¯g+​(θ)⟩<0\langle\bar{v}_{g^{-}}(\theta),\bar{v}_{g^{+}}(\theta)\rangle<0). Uniform pooling or symmetric gradient surgery (PCGrad [43]) gives incompatible and transferable teachers equal priority, attenuating v¯g+​(θ)\bar{v}_{g^{+}}(\theta). Resolving this conflict requires reweighting teachers asymmetrically before gradient aggregation, yet estimating inter-teacher compatibility without target data is non-trivial because rule teacher τg​(st)\tau_{g}(s_{t}) depends on private simulator state and cannot run on peer games g′≠gg^{\prime}\neq g.

Cross-source specialist disagreement probing.

To bypass private simulator states, we use the frozen visual specialist probes {πTg}\{\pi_{T_{g}}\} trained in Sec. 3.2 as pixel-based proxies for {τg}\{\tau_{g}\}. Without requiring identical action names or hand-crafted aliases, 1/La1/L_{a} normalization removes multi-token bias on 𝒜g′\mathcal{A}_{g^{\prime}} (restoring a calibrated base-VLM prior) while using pretrained verb semantics. Because 1M​∑gγg=1\frac{1}{M}\sum_{g}\gamma_{g}=1 with γg+>1>γg−\gamma_{g^{+}}>1>\gamma_{g^{-}}, Eq. 9 upweights compatible corrections and suppresses conflicting ones (β=0\beta=0 recovers uniform MOPD). The multiplier γg\gamma_{g} scales only the on-policy term: consolidation starts from θSFT\theta_{\mathrm{SFT}} under ℒanchor\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anchor}}, so v¯0​(θ)\bar{v}_{0}(\theta) on 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} is near saturation and maintains the shared visual representation, whereas wq​∑gγg​v¯g​(θ)w_{q}\sum_{g}\gamma_{g}\bar{v}_{g}(\theta) sets boundary recovery without discarding offline samples. Finally, to absorb reweighted corrections while limiting policy drift from θref=θSFT\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}=\theta_{\mathrm{SFT}}, we update θ\theta on minibatches i∼Pglobali\sim P_{\mathrm{global}} via the anchored loss (λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, Tref>0T_{\mathrm{ref}}>0):

ℒ⁡(θ)=ℒaction​(θ)+λ​ℒanchor​(θ),ℒaction​(θ)=𝔼i∼Pglobal​[−log⁡πθ​(ai⋆∣xi,𝒜gi)],ℒanchor​(θ)=𝔼i∼Pglobal​[Tref2​KL​(πθref(Tref)​(xi)∥πθ(Tref)​(xi))],\begin{split}\mathcal{L}(\theta)&=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}(\theta)+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anchor}}(\theta),\\ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}(\theta)&=\mathbb{E}_{i\sim P_{\mathrm{global}}}\!\left[-\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{i}^{\star}\mid x_{i},\mathcal{A}_{g_{i}})\right]\!,\\ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anchor}}(\theta)&=\mathbb{E}_{i\sim P_{\mathrm{global}}}\!\left[T_{\mathrm{ref}}^{2}\,\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}}^{(T_{\mathrm{ref}})}(x_{i})\,\middle\|\,\pi_{\theta}^{(T_{\mathrm{ref}})}(x_{i})\right)\right]\!,\end{split} (10)

where π(Tref)​(xi)\pi^{(T_{\mathrm{ref}})}(x_{i}) abbreviates π(Tref)(⋅∣xi,𝒜gi)\pi^{(T_{\mathrm{ref}})}(\cdot\mid x_{i},\mathcal{A}_{g_{i}}), KL(⋅∥⋅)\mathrm{KL}(\cdot\|\cdot) is the Kullback–Leibler divergence, and Tref2T_{\mathrm{ref}}^{2} preserves gradient scale. Matching the full reference distribution via ℒanchor\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anchor}} prevents entropy collapse under amplified boundary updates (wq​γgw_{q}\gamma_{g}). At deployment, all teachers and probes are discarded, leaving one consolidated student πθ\pi_{\theta}.

4 Experiments

We evaluate CAMOPD on unseen target games under GameWorld’s Paused 100-Step Reset-on-Fail protocol [23].

4.1 Experimental Setup and Baselines

Environments and evaluation protocol.

As summarized in Table 1, Suite A evaluates temporal intervention transfer from Boxel Rebound and Stack to held-out GeoDash (𝒜g⋆={wait,jump}\mathcal{A}_{g^{\star}}=\{\texttt{wait},\texttt{jump}\}, h=1h{=}1), while Suite B evaluates directional steering transfer from Breakout, NS-Shaft, and Cubefield to held-out Doodle Jump (𝒜g⋆={wait,move_left,move_right}\mathcal{A}_{g^{\star}}=\{\texttt{wait},\texttt{move\_left},\texttt{move\_right}\}, h=2h{=}2). Each episode launches a fresh browser instance, pauses the simulator during VLM inference, and executes up to 100 closed-loop decisions, resetting upon terminal failure. We evaluate Tasks 1 and 2 over 30 executions each and report success rate (SR), peak progress (PG, %), T1–T2 mean, and Resets↓\downarrow.

Implementation details.

All methods share Qwen3.5-4B with rank-16 LoRA [12] on attention and MLP projections (sequence length 2048, 65,536–401,408 pixels), optimized using AdamW (T=Tref=1T=T_{\mathrm{ref}}=1). Selective retention uses cmin=0.75c_{\min}=0.75 and δ=0.25\delta=0.25, while conflict-aware consolidation uses β=1\beta=1, ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1, cfloor=0.05c_{\mathrm{floor}}=0.05, and wq=3w_{q}=3; we set the anchor weight and learning rate to λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 and 10−510^{-5} for Suite A, and to λ=1.0\lambda=1.0 and 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} for Suite B.

Baselines.

We compare CAMOPD against four baseline families (Table 2): (i) Prompted VLMs: Base VLM, Pause-and-Plan chain-of-thought (CoT) [34], and few-shot in-context learning (ICL); (ii) Single-teacher specialists trained on each source game; (iii) Parameter-space mergers: Task Arithmetic [14], TIES-Merging [39], DARE-TIES [42], DELLA [7], Model Stock [15], and RegMean (diagonal) [16]; and (iv) Multi-teacher optimization and routing: Multi-Task PCGrad [43] and Feature-Routing MoE [20].

4.2 Main Cross-Game Transfer Results

Tables 2 and 2 summarize zero-shot transfer performance and representative closed-loop rollouts across both suites. Because reaching the Task-1 target requires ∼75{\sim}75–8080 steps (Fig. 2(a4, b4)), the doubled Task-2 thresholds (Table 1) exceed the physical reach of the 100-step horizon, yielding 0/30 Task-2 SR across all methods and differentiating long-horizon control through Task-2 PG.

Performance on Suite A (temporal control).

On GeoDash, zero-shot Base VLM triggers premature jumps, crashing into spikes at t≈68t\approx 68 and resetting to 0%0\% in Fig. 2(a4) (0/30 Task-1 SR), while prompted VLMs (Pause-and-Plan CoT at 13/30 SR, 73.8 Mean PG; Few-shot ICL at 5/30 SR) remain sensitive to timing drift. Single-source specialists expose the underlying teacher conflict: Boxel Rebound transfers reactive obstacle-jumping timing (14/30 SR, 67.0 Mean PG), whereas Stack reflects block-alignment dynamics that fail to transfer (0/30 SR)—as failed attempts respawn right before the first spike and crash within two decisions, mis-timed jumps incur ∼3,000{\sim}3{,}000 resets across the 6,000 total steps of Tasks 1–2. Because Multi-Task PCGrad projects conflicting gradients onto normal planes with equal task priority, updates from Stack attenuate transferable timing signals (0/30 SR), while parameter mergers (peaking at 19/30 SR for TIES-Merging and 73.3 Mean PG for DELLA) and Feature-Routing MoE (17/30 SR) still suffer from adapter interference. In contrast, by resolving teacher conflict in aligned action space rather than blending divergent weights, CAMOPD waits on flat segments and jumps cleanly over hazards (Fig. 2(a1–a3)), reaching the Task-1 threshold in Fig. 2(a4) with 26/30 Task-1 SR, 76.7 Mean PG, and the fewest resets (36)—outperforming the strongest baselines in both success rate (19/30 for TIES-Merging) and progress (73.8 Mean PG for CoT).

Performance on Suite B (directional steering).

Suite B requires sustained lateral alignment with ascending platforms on Doodle Jump (Fig. 2(b1–b4)). Prompted VLMs reach at most 12/30 Task-1 SR (Few-shot ICL, 48.1 Mean PG), while among source specialists, NS-Shaft shares compatible platform-landing dynamics (6/30 SR) whereas Breakout and Cubefield fail to transfer (0/30 SR). Interpolating LoRA deltas in parameter space (Task Arithmetic, TIES-Merging, DARE-TIES, DELLA, RegMean) implicitly assumes linear connectivity [10]; combining NS-Shaft with opposing steering adapters cancels lateral control, leaving policies bouncing in place on the starting platform (0% PG and thus 0 fall resets), while Multi-Task PCGrad (0/30 SR) and test-time Feature-Routing MoE (4/30 SR under visual shift) likewise struggle. In Fig. 2(b4), Base VLM stalls near the bottom and Action-aligned SFT falls at t=50t=50 after drifting off-course; in contrast, CAMOPD suppresses conflicting corrections in action space to correct lateral drift (Fig. 2(b1–b3)) and reach 100%100\% progress (Fig. 2(b4)), attaining 24/30 Task-1 SR (65.7 Mean PG, 12 resets) and doubling the strongest baseline SR (Few-shot ICL, 12/30).

4.3 Ablation Studies

Effect of complete-action alignment.

Table 3 evaluates each component from offline Token SFT, which exhibits marked closed-loop instability (462 and 85 resets in Suites A and B) as subword cross-entropy biases predictions toward shorter or lexically favored strings. Normalizing command completion likelihoods over each game’s legal action set 𝒜g\mathcal{A}_{g} via Complete-Action Alignment mitigates subword length bias and forms a calibrated categorical policy, cutting Suite A resets from 462 to 57 (Task-1 SR 0/30→11/300/30{\to}11/30) and lifting Suite B Mean PG from 40.7 to 46.8, though offline alignment remains prone to rollout drift (2/30 Suite-B SR).

Effect of selective on-policy retention.

Adding Selective MOPD (Uniform) uses these calibrated uncertainty margins to retain teacher corrections 𝒬\mathcal{Q} on student-visited error and low-margin states, consolidating 𝒟0∪𝒬\mathcal{D}_{0}\cup\mathcal{Q} under Eq. 10 with equal teacher weights (γg=1\gamma_{g}{=}1). Supervising such boundary states mitigates rollout drift in Suite B, lifting Task-1 SR from 2/30 to 8/30 and cutting resets (71→4171{\to}41). However, uniform pooling over 𝒬\mathcal{Q} exposes multi-teacher policy conflict: in Suite A, incompatible corrections from Stack interfere with Boxel Rebound’s jump timing and drop Task-1 SR from 11/30 to 7/30, while in Suite B opposing steering signals from Breakout and Cubefield lower Task-1 PG from 65.9 to 57.7, motivating conflict-aware reweighting over 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

Effect of conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation.

Incorporating Conflict-Aware Consolidation (Full CAMOPD) resolves conflict in 𝒟0∪𝒬\mathcal{D}_{0}\cup\mathcal{Q} without target data by cross-evaluating the aligned specialists to upweight compatible teachers and suppress conflicting corrections, lifting Task-1 SR from 7/30→𝟐𝟔/𝟑𝟎7/30{\to}\mathbf{26/30} (63.5→76.763.5{\to}\mathbf{76.7} Mean PG; resets 87→𝟑𝟔87{\to}\mathbf{36}) in Suite A and 8/30→𝟐𝟒/𝟑𝟎8/30{\to}\mathbf{24/30} (49.8→65.749.8{\to}\mathbf{65.7} Mean PG; resets 41→𝟏𝟐41{\to}\mathbf{12}) in Suite B. Selective MOPD’s higher Suite B Task-2 PG reflects peak-bounce variance across 41 resets (vs. 12) rather than sustained climbing.

5 Further Analysis and Generalization

5.1 Multi-Teacher Policy Conflict Analysis

Asymmetric inter-teacher disagreement.

Table 4 inspects Cg,g′C_{g,g^{\prime}} and γg\gamma_{g} (Eqs. 7 and 8). In Suite A, Boxel Rebound fits its own states far more reliably than Stack (0.0590.059 vs. 0.4680.468 diagonal NLL) and incurs lower cross-game loss (0.7060.706 vs. 0.8060.806), yielding lower C¯g\bar{C}_{g} (0.3830.383 vs. 0.6370.637) as in-game reliability and peer compatibility both favor Boxel Rebound. In Suite B, Breakout includes additional rare long-stroke moves (*_long; Table S3), and predicting wall-bounced ball paths from two frames is visually ambiguous. Consequently, πTBreakout\pi_{T_{\text{Breakout}}} assigns near-zero probability to rare *_long moves on the action-balanced validation split (3.0503.050 NLL vs. 2.6102.610 for πTNS-Shaft\pi_{T_{\text{NS-Shaft}}}, which does not suppress unseen *_long actions), whereas NS-Shaft fits its own three-action control cleanly (0.0500.050). Meanwhile, Cubefield fits its own dodging (0.5620.562) yet incurs 2.0982.098 on NS-Shaft from opposing rules (dodging vs. platform landing).

Target-free teacher identification.

Computed solely from source validation splits, the inferred weights γg\gamma_{g} accurately reflect standalone zero-shot transfer (Table 2): in Suite A, Boxel Rebound is upweighted over Stack (γg=1.69\gamma_{g}{=}1.69 vs. 0.310.31, corresponding to 67.067.0 vs. 22.522.5 Mean PG on GeoDash); in Suite B, NS-Shaft (γg=2.00\gamma_{g}{=}2.00) is prioritized over Breakout (0.740.74) and Cubefield (0.260.26), mirroring their standalone Mean PG of 44.144.1, 7.17.1, and 0.00.0 on Doodle Jump. Moreover, multi-teacher consolidation markedly outperforms the strongest standalone specialist in each suite (26/30 vs. 14/30 Task-1 SR in Suite A; 24/30 vs. 6/30 in Suite B): retaining 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} with prior floor ϵ=0.1\epsilon{=}0.1 preserves multi-game visual diversity while selectively suppressing conflicting boundary updates.

5.2 Causal Visual Interventions

Table 5 tests whether transfer relies on live visual feedback rather than open-loop priors. Vision-free controls fail to sustain play: constant wait stalls, while a fixed periodic cycle inflates Suite A Task-2 PG only via 313 crash resets (8.7×8.7\times CAMOPD), dropping Task-1 SR to 16/30 in Suite A and 0/30 in Suite B. Crucially, freezing input at the initial frame o0o_{0} collapses Task-1 SR from 26/30 to 1/30 in Suite A and from 24/30 to 0/30 in Suite B. These results confirm that live visual feedback is essential for closed-loop timing and drift correction, and show that CAMOPD grounds decisions in visual dynamics rather than action rhythms.

5.3 Cross-Genre Distance and Transfer Boundaries

Fig. 3 examines cross-genre transfer across six unseen target games as a function of the action–dynamics distance d⁡(𝒢src,g⋆)=12​(dact+ddyn)d(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}},g^{\star})=\frac{1}{2}(d_{\mathrm{act}}+d_{\mathrm{dyn}}) (Appendix B). Overall, transfer gains tend to diminish as d⁡(𝒢src,g⋆)d(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}},g^{\star}) increases. Within Suite A, progress gain decreases monotonically with distance from Core Ball (d=0.466d{=}0.466, +19.8+19.8 PG) to GeoDash (d=0.502d{=}0.502, +7.7+7.7 PG) and Chrome Dino (d=0.596d{=}0.596, +3.9+3.9 PG). In Suite B, gains similarly decline from Doodle Jump (d=0.232d{=}0.232, +25.4+25.4 PG) to Pac-Man (d=0.339d{=}0.339, +12.7+12.7 PG). Notably, Edge Surf (d=0.336d{=}0.336) achieves a larger +46.9+46.9 PG gain, as its obstacle-avoidance dynamics closely match the consolidated lateral steering prior.

6 Conclusion

We present CAMOPD, a conflict-aware multi-teacher on-policy distillation framework that consolidates heterogeneous source teachers into a single pixel-only VLM without target data. Built on length-normalized complete-action distributions, CAMOPD retains boundary corrections via calibrated margins and cross-evaluates visual specialist probes across peer source games to upweight compatible teachers and suppress conflicting updates. On GameWorld’s temporal and directional suites, CAMOPD reaches 86.7% and 80.0% Task-1 zero-shot success, surpassing prompting, single-teacher, merging, and multi-task methods.

7 Limitations

First, following GameWorld [23], evaluation pauses execution during inference over discrete commands rather than real-time continuous streams. Second, the student conditions on a short hh-frame window (h∈{1,2}h\in\{1,2\}) without explicit long-horizon episodic memory. Extending CAMOPD to streaming control and memory-augmented policies remains future work; further exploring state-adaptive compatibility weighting beyond source-level γg\gamma_{g} is also a promising direction.

Appendix A Algorithm Pseudocode

Algorithm 1 summarizes the end-to-end training and zero-shot deployment pipeline of CAMOPD (Sec. 3).

Output: Consolidated pixel-only student policy πθ\pi_{\theta} for zero-shot deployment on unseen target games g⋆∉𝒢srcg^{\star}\notin\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}.
Complete-Action Alignment (Sec. 3.2)
1: Roll out each teacher τg​(st)→(at⋆,ct)\tau_{g}(s_{t})\to(a_{t}^{\star},c_{t}) on g∈𝒢srcg\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}} to collect offline bank 𝒟0=⋃g∈𝒢src𝒟g\mathcal{D}_{0}=\bigcup_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}}\mathcal{D}_{g} and action-balanced validation splits {𝒟gval}g∈𝒢src\{\mathcal{D}_{g}^{\mathrm{val}}\}_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}}.

3: Define calibrated categorical policy πθ(T)​(a∣x,𝒜g)=exp⁡(sθ​(a∣x)/T)/∑a′∈𝒜gexp⁡(sθ​(a′∣x)/T)\pi_{\theta}^{(T)}(a\mid x,\mathcal{A}_{g})=\exp(s_{\theta}(a\mid x)/T)\big/\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}_{g}}\exp(s_{\theta}(a^{\prime}\mid x)/T) ⊳\triangleright Eq. 3

Appendix B Action–Dynamics Domain Distance Formulation

To characterize cross-genre transfer boundaries in Sec. 5.3 and Fig. 3, we collect short uniform-random rollouts {(ot,at,ot′)}\{(o_{t},a_{t},o^{\prime}_{t})\} separate from policy training and extract ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized visual embeddings ϕ⁡(o)∈ℝd\phi(o)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} using the frozen Qwen3.5-4B vision tower. For any pair of games (gi,gj)(g_{i},g_{j}), we compute two complementary distance axes:

  1. 1.

    Action-semantic distance (dactd_{\mathrm{act}}): mapping surface commands in 𝒜g\mathcal{A}_{g} to coarse control roles (wait, vertical/event triggers, lateral/vertical turns), we take an equal-weight combination of role-set Jaccard distance between 𝒜gi\mathcal{A}_{g_{i}} and 𝒜gj\mathcal{A}_{g_{j}} and the normalized cosine distance between role-conditioned feature displacements 𝔼⁡[ϕ⁡(ot′)−ϕ⁡(ot)∣e]\mathbb{E}[\phi(o^{\prime}_{t})-\phi(o_{t})\mid e] matched across shared roles ee (1.01.0 if disjoint).

  2. 2.

    Transition dynamics distance (ddynd_{\mathrm{dyn}}): squared maximum mean discrepancy (MMD2\mathrm{MMD}^{2}) with a Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) kernel over frame-to-frame transition vectors Δ​ϕt=ϕ⁡(ot′)−ϕ⁡(ot)\Delta\phi_{t}=\phi(o^{\prime}_{t})-\phi(o_{t}), capturing temporal motion similarity.

Normalizing each axis to [0,1][0,1] across evaluated game pairs yields the pairwise and suite-to-target action–dynamics distance:

d⁡(gi,gj)=12​(dact​(gi,gj)+ddyn​(gi,gj)),d⁡(𝒢src,g⋆)=1|𝒢src|​∑g∈𝒢srcd⁡(g,g⋆).\begin{split}d(g_{i},g_{j})&=\tfrac{1}{2}\big(d_{\mathrm{act}}(g_{i},g_{j})+d_{\mathrm{dyn}}(g_{i},g_{j})\big),\\ d(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}},g^{\star})&=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}|}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}}d(g,g^{\star}).\end{split} (11)

Intuitively, Eq. 11 focuses on functional control mechanics rather than static appearance: pretrained VLM encoders already generalize across background colors and sprite textures, whereas zero-shot policy transfer hinges on whether actions induce comparable visual displacements (dactd_{\mathrm{act}}) under similar frame-to-frame motion pacing (ddynd_{\mathrm{dyn}}). Small values on both axes indicate that consolidated timing or steering priors act on aligned transition dynamics, whereas additional target control roles (larger dactd_{\mathrm{act}}) or shifted motion distributions (larger ddynd_{\mathrm{dyn}}) narrow the transferable skill subspace, and averaging over g∈𝒢srcg\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}} summarizes proximity to the multi-source pool. Note that d⁡(𝒢src,g⋆)d(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}},g^{\star}) is computed only for post-hoc analysis of unseen target games and is not used during student training or conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation. Table S1 reports the native action sets, per-axis distances, and zero-shot T1–T2 Mean PG across all six unseen target games; during cross-genre evaluation, each suite scores the target game’s native temporal (Core Ball: {wait, shoot}, Chrome Dino: {wait, jump}) or lateral (Edge Surf: {wait, turn_left/right}, Pac-Man: {wait, move_left/right}) command subset matching the source control axis.

Appendix C Prompt Template and Privileged Source Teachers

Prompt template and complete-action completion scoring.

In Complete-Action Alignment (Sec. 3.2), each multimodal context xt=(ot−h+1:t,qg)x_{t}=(o_{t-h+1:t},q_{g}) is formatted under Qwen3.5-4B’s chat template with reasoning disabled (enable_thinking=False) so that inference and training operate on executable semantic commands. Table S2 illustrates the prompt structure and how Complete-Action Alignment (Eq. 2) scores the legal command completion tokens y⁡(a)y(a) while masking prompt tokens.

Privileged source rule teachers.

During source data collection only (g∈𝒢srcg\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{src}}), each source game is paired with a programmatic rule teacher τg​(st)→(at⋆,ct)\tau_{g}(s_{t})\to(a_{t}^{\star},c_{t}) that reads simulator state variables st∈𝒮gs_{t}\in\mathcal{S}_{g} and outputs reference action at⋆∈𝒜ga_{t}^{\star}\in\mathcal{A}_{g} along with criticality confidence ct∈(0,1]c_{t}\in(0,1] (cmin=0.75c_{\min}=0.75). Table S3 summarizes the privileged state inputs, decision rules, and confidence assignments of all five source teachers across Suites A and B.
